source_read: PDF (scan), pp. 103–110 (all 8 pages). The OCR text layer was used only to search; every number was read on pages rendered at 150 dpi, and Tables 1 and 2 (p. 107) on a 300-dpi render. The text layer misreads several table cells (Table 1: Total at onset 13 is printed 47.3, OCR 41.3; Black at 15 27.4, OCR 21.4; Male at 25 or older 9.7, OCR 9.1; Nonblack at 25 or older 7.7, OCR 1.7; Table 2: Black at 15 9.7, OCR 9.1), so a mechanical text-layer check of an anchor quoting 47.3 on p. 107 will fail although the value is correct.

claims.overstatement: One phrase overstates the source: 'conduct problems, other psychiatric disorders, family environment and other drug use were not measured'. This paper shows only that these were not used or adjusted for. The survey did measure other drug use: the AUDADIS reliability study it cites covered the alcohol and drug modules (p. 109, references), and the claim itself sends readers to the same survey's analysis of other drugs (Grant & Dawson, 1998). Suggested wording: 'were not taken into account in this analysis'. The rest of the claim's account of this source is accurate and appropriately hedged.
claims.note: Supported from this source: NLAES 1992, 42,862 adults interviewed once, about 92% of selected households and 97.4% of selected respondents (p. 104); 27,616 current (18,352) and former (9,264) drinkers (p. 106); the onset question excluded tastes or sips (p. 105); Table 1 Total column all 14 values with the three SEs quoted, read on the rendered page (40.6, 47.3, 40.8, 38.7, 30.6, 24.5, 16.6, 16.5, 11.4, 10.0, 9.5, 14.7, 13.6, 7.9); abuse without dependence 8.3–13.8% at 16 or younger, peak 13.8% at 14, 2.5% at 25 or older (Table 2); adjusted odds 14% and 8% lower per year with the six covariates as listed, and no ORs, CIs, p values or unadjusted estimates (pp. 106, 108); the editors' conversion to about 0.86 and 0.92 is right; the authors' description of onset age as a powerful predictor and of ages 16 and younger as a particularly vulnerable period (p. 108), and the closing paragraph's statement that the delay itself or, more likely, other associated factors may explain the link, with a call for a prospective study (p. 109). Inferences that are reasonable but not stated in the paper: 'often decades later' (respondents were 18 to over 65; the age distribution of drinkers is not given), and the exclusion of people who had died or were homeless (the paper says household sampling of the noninstitutionalized population of the contiguous US and DC). The point that two adjustments may follow from the disorder is supported by the definitions on pp. 105–106. One more point the claim could add: duration of drinking is age at interview (or last drink) minus age at onset, so adjusting for both age group and duration leaves the onset term partly tied to duration; the authors themselves say onset and duration still need to be disentangled (p. 109). No dosing or advice content in the claim. The paper's own suggestion to delay drinking until after 18 or 19 (pp. 108–109) is correctly left out of the claim.

anchors.extracted: NLAES, NIAAA-sponsored, fieldwork by the Census Bureau in 1992: face-to-face interviews with 42,862 adults aged 18 and over in the noninstitutionalized population of the contiguous US and DC; about 92% of selected households and 97.4% of selected respondents in them took part; multistage design with oversampling of Black and young adult (18–29) respondents.

Lifetime DSM-IV alcohol dependence and abuse from the AUDADIS (episode in the past year or before), mutually exclusive (abuse = abuse without lifetime dependence); test-retest reliability 0.76 and 0.73. Onset: how old the respondent was when first starting to drink, not counting small tastes or sips (test-retest 0.72). Covariates race, sex, age group (18–24, 25–44, 45–64, 65+) and duration of drinking = age at last drink (former drinkers) or at interview (current) minus onset age, 0.5 years if equal.

Family history positive if any of 18 types of first- or second-degree relative was reported as an alcoholic or problem drinker. Logistic regression of lifetime abuse or dependence on onset age, controlling for sex, race, age, duration of drinking, family history and current (past-year) vs former drinking; SUDAAN for the complex design.

Analysis base: 27,616 current (18,352) and former (9,264) drinkers. More than 40% of those starting before 15 had lifetime dependence, 38.7% and 30.6% at 15 and 16, 24.5% at 17, about 10% at 21 and 22 (the text places the later rise at 22 and 23; the table shows it at 23 and 24).

Weighted prevalence (SE) of lifetime dependence by recalled age at first drink: 12 or younger 40.6 (2.1); 13 47.3 (2.7); 14 40.8 (1.9); 15 38.7 (1.4); 16 30.6 (0.9); 17 24.5 (1.0); 18 16.6 (0.6); 19 16.5 (1.0); 20 11.4 (0.8); 21 10.0 (0.6); 22 9.5 (1.1); 23 14.7 (1.9); 24 13.6 (2.1); 25 or older 7.9 (0.6). Read on the 300-dpi render (the text layer gives 41.3 for onset 13). Numbers per onset age not given.

Weighted prevalence (SE) of lifetime abuse without dependence: 12 or younger 8.3 (1.1); 13 11.5 (1.8); 14 13.8 (1.5); 15 11.9 (0.9); 16 10.6 (0.7); falling to 4.8 (0.5) at 20 and 2.5 (0.4) at 25 or older.

Onset entered as a continuous term; after adjustment, odds of lifetime dependence 14% lower and of lifetime abuse 8% lower per later year of onset (about 0.86 and 0.92 as odds ratios, my conversion); subgroups: dependence 14.7% (men), 13.2% (women), 14.5% (nonblack), 8.1% (Black); abuse 7.0%, 9.1%, 6.7%, 7.8%. No odds ratios, intervals, p values or unadjusted estimates printed.

Authors call age at first use a powerful predictor; the rise from 9.5% (22) to 14.7% and 13.6% (23, 24) is attributed, without data, to possible psychopathology; ages 16 and younger called a particularly vulnerable period; a prevention focus on delaying onset is suggested but to be considered cautiously because why onset relates to the disorders is not understood.

A prospective study is needed to tell whether the delay itself or, more likely, other associated factors explain the inverse relationship, whether early onset is a modifiable risk factor or a marker, and to reduce the recall bias of cross-sectional designs including this one and to disentangle onset age from duration of drinking.

anchors.locator: References, Grant, Harford, Dawson, Chou & Pickering (1995)
anchors.extracted: The cited AUDADIS reliability study covered alcohol and drug modules: the survey instrument included drug use, which this analysis did not use (relevant to the claim's 'not measured').

key_findings.note: All 14 values and SEs match my 300-dpi reading; the 41.3/47.3 text-layer error confirmed.
Men's value exceeds women's in all 14 rows; Black column min 9.5 (22), max 44.4 (13); the four text-layer misreads confirmed.

reporting_issues.note: Ranges reproduced: abuse 8.3–13.8 (16 or younger), 2.5–4.9 (20 or older); dependence 7.9–14.7 (20 or older).

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high, driven by confounding, is right. Wording correction for the confounding note (and for cannot_establish and comparison.unmeasured_premorbid): other drug use, and possibly other psychopathology, were not used or adjusted for in this analysis. 'Not measured' is not supported: the AUDADIS reliability study cited on p. 109 covered drug modules, and the same survey's drug analysis is grant_1998 (already in the card's timeline). The polysubstance field's 'neither measured in this analysis nor adjusted for' is the accurate form.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is defensible because the closing paragraph concedes that other factors more likely explain the link. Moderate would also be defensible: the Results' 'major contributor to the development' (p. 108) and the age thresholds for prevention read causation into a cross-sectional association.

missed: 'Not measured' versus 'not used' (see risk_of_bias note): p. 109 references show that the AUDADIS had drug modules; fix the three card fields that say other drug use was not measured.

pp. 105–106 with p. 109: for current drinkers, duration of drinking = age at interview minus onset age, so adjusting for age group and duration together leaves the per-year onset estimate conditional on duration and partly confounded with it, not a total association. The authors say onset and duration still need to be disentangled (p. 109). RI4 covers duration only as a possible consequence of the disorder.
p. 108: the comparison group for the abuse model (no disorder, or everyone without abuse including people with dependence) is not stated, so the 8% figure is hard to interpret; minor.
